title.en: Section 1 - Conversation at a Health Club
title.zh: 第一部分 - 健身俱乐部对话

sections.passage: A conversation between a new member, Sarah, and a receptionist at a health club. Sarah has just moved to the area and wants to join a gym. The receptionist, Mike, welcomes her and explains the different membership options available. The club offers three tiers: Basic, Standard, and Premium. The Basic membership costs 35 pounds per month and includes access to the gym floor and swimming pool. The Standard membership is 55 pounds per month and adds access to group fitness classes, the sauna, and the steam room. The Premium membership costs 80 pounds per month and includes all facilities plus personal training sessions twice a month. Sarah mentions that she is particularly interested in yoga classes. Mike tells her that yoga is offered three times a week: on Monday and Wednesday evenings at 6:30 PM, and on Saturday mornings at 10 AM. He also mentions that they have recently introduced a new Pilates class on Thursday evenings. Sarah asks about the contract length, and Mike explains that the minimum commitment is three months, but they offer a 15 percent discount for annual memberships paid upfront. There is also a one-time registration fee of 25 pounds, but this is waived for members who sign up during the promotional period, which ends on the 30th of this month. Sarah decides to go with the Standard membership on a monthly basis initially, and Mike gives her a membership card and a welcome pack containing information about class schedules and club rules.

title.en: Section 2 - Introduction to a Wildlife Sanctuary
title.zh: 第二部分 - 野生动物保护区介绍

sections.passage: Welcome to Greenfield Wildlife Sanctuary. My name is David Thompson, and I'm the senior ranger here. Before we begin our guided tour, I'd like to give you some important information about the sanctuary and its facilities. Greenfield was established in 1985 and covers an area of 450 hectares of mixed woodland, grassland, and wetland habitats. We are home to over 200 species of birds, 35 species of mammals, and numerous reptiles and amphibians. The sanctuary is open to visitors from 9 AM to 5 PM daily, with last entry at 4 PM. Admission is 12 pounds for adults, 8 pounds for children aged 5 to 16, and free for children under 5. Family tickets for two adults and up to three children cost 32 pounds, which represents a saving of 8 pounds compared to individual tickets. We have three marked walking trails. The Woodland Trail is the shortest at 2 kilometres and takes approximately one hour to complete. It is wheelchair accessible and suitable for all ages. The Lakeside Trail is 4 kilometres long and passes by our main bird-watching hides, where you can observe herons, kingfishers, and in spring, nesting swans. The longest trail is the Moorland Trail at 7 kilometres, which offers panoramic views of the surrounding countryside but involves some steep sections and is recommended for experienced walkers only. Our visitor centre includes a cafe serving hot and cold meals, a gift shop, and an exhibition hall featuring interactive displays about local wildlife. For families, we offer special activity packs for children at 3 pounds each, which include binoculars hire, a wildlife spotting guide, and a certificate. Please note that dogs are not permitted on the trails except for registered assistance animals. Photography is welcome, but flash photography is prohibited near the bird hides to avoid disturbing the wildlife.

title.en: Section 3 - Tutorial on Marine Biology Research
title.zh: 第三部分 - 海洋生物学研究辅导

sections.passage: A tutorial between a student, Emma, and her supervisor, Professor Roberts, about Emma's dissertation on the impact of microplastics on marine ecosystems. Emma has completed her literature review and is now planning her field research methodology. Professor Roberts asks Emma to summarize her key findings from the literature review. Emma explains that microplastics, defined as plastic particles smaller than 5 millimetres, have been found in virtually every marine environment studied, from surface waters to deep-sea sediments. She mentions that recent estimates suggest there are over 170 trillion plastic particles floating in the world's oceans. Professor Roberts is impressed with the breadth of Emma's reading but cautions her about relying too heavily on secondary sources. He recommends that she include more primary research papers published in the last three years. They then discuss Emma's proposed methodology. She plans to collect water and sediment samples from three coastal sites along the south coast of England over a six-month period. Each site will be sampled monthly, with three replicates taken at each visit. Professor Roberts suggests adding a fourth site as a control location, perhaps an area that has relatively low human activity. Emma agrees and mentions a remote bay in Cornwall that might be suitable. They also discuss the analytical techniques. Emma plans to use Fourier Transform Infrared Spectroscopy, commonly known as FTIR, to identify the types of plastic present in her samples. Professor Roberts recommends also using a scanning electron microscope to examine the surface texture of the particles, which can provide clues about how long they have been in the marine environment. The supervisor asks about the timeline, and Emma says she aims to complete all fieldwork by the end of March and have her analysis done by May, leaving June and July for writing up her findings. The final submission deadline is the 15th of August.

title.en: Section 4 - Lecture on the History of Cartography
title.zh: 第四部分 - 关于制图学历史的讲座

sections.passage: Good afternoon. Today's lecture continues our series on the history of science and exploration, and I'll be focusing on cartography — the art and science of map-making. Maps have been fundamental to human civilization, serving as tools for navigation, land ownership, military strategy, and the expression of worldviews. The earliest known maps date back to ancient Babylon, around 2300 BC. These were clay tablets depicting local land boundaries and celestial patterns. The ancient Greeks made enormous contributions to cartography. Eratosthenes, who lived in the third century BC, calculated the circumference of the Earth with remarkable accuracy using observations of shadows at different latitudes. His estimate was within approximately 2 percent of the modern accepted value. The Greek geographer Ptolemy, working in the second century AD, created a comprehensive world map and wrote the Geography, a guide to map-making that influenced cartographers for over a thousand years. During the medieval period in Europe, cartography was dominated by religious worldviews. The most common type of map was the Mappa Mundi, which placed Jerusalem at the centre of the world and was more concerned with theological symbolism than geographical accuracy. Meanwhile, Islamic cartographers were making significant advances. Al-Idrisi, working at the court of the Norman king Roger II in Sicily, produced the Tabula Rogeriana in 1154, which was the most accurate world map of its time and remained influential for three centuries. The Age of Exploration in the 15th and 16th centuries revolutionized map-making. The development of the portolan chart, which showed detailed coastlines and compass bearings, enabled sailors to navigate across open oceans with unprecedented accuracy. Gerardus Mercator's projection of 1569 solved the problem of representing a curved surface on a flat map and remains the basis for most world maps today. The 18th and 19th centuries saw the rise of systematic national surveys. The Ordnance Survey in Britain, founded in 1791, produced detailed topographical maps that set new standards for accuracy. Today, cartography has entered the digital age with Geographic Information Systems, or GIS, allowing us to create, analyze, and share spatial data in ways that Eratosthenes could never have imagined.

title.en: Passage 1 - The Development of the London Underground
title.zh: 文章1 - 伦敦地铁的发展

sections.passage:
The London Underground, affectionately known as the Tube, is the world's oldest underground railway. Its history is a fascinating story of Victorian engineering ambition, urban growth, and technological innovation. The idea of an underground railway in London was first proposed in the 1830s, but it was not until 1863 that the Metropolitan Railway opened the world's first underground railway line, running between Paddington and Farringdon Street. The line was built using a method known as cut-and-cover, in which a deep trench was dug along the route of the road above, the sides were supported with brick walls, and then the trench was roofed over with iron girders and the road was replaced on top. This initial line was an immediate success, carrying 38,000 passengers on its first day of operation.

The early underground railways were hauled by steam locomotives, which naturally produced smoke and steam in the enclosed tunnels. Ventilation was a constant problem, with stations designed with open gratings in the road above to allow fumes to escape. Despite these uncomfortable conditions, the network expanded rapidly. The Metropolitan District Railway, now part of the District line, was completed in 1884, creating what was known as the Inner Circle. By the end of the 19th century, several more lines had been opened, all using the same cut-and-cover construction method.

The introduction of electric traction in 1890 marked a revolutionary change. The City and South London Railway, now part of the Northern line, was the first deep-level electric railway in the world. Electric locomotives were cleaner, faster, and more powerful than steam engines, and they could operate in smaller, circular tunnels that were bored through the London clay rather than cut from the surface. This tunnelling technique was significantly cheaper than cut-and-cover and caused far less disruption to the streets above. The success of electric traction led to a second wave of underground railway construction in the early 20th century, with several new deep-level lines being opened.

The iconic London Underground map that we recognize today was designed by Harry Beck in 1931. Beck, an engineering draftsman, realized that passengers were less interested in geographical accuracy than in understanding how to get from one station to another. His revolutionary design abandoned the traditional approach of showing the lines in their correct geographical positions and instead used a diagrammatic style with horizontal, vertical, and 45-degree diagonal lines. The map was initially rejected by the London Underground management as too revolutionary, but when it was finally published in 1933, it proved enormously popular with the public and has been the basis for the Tube map ever since.

Today, the London Underground carries over 1.3 billion passenger journeys per year across 11 lines, serving 272 stations. It remains an essential part of London's transport infrastructure and continues to evolve, with the Elizabeth line, which opened in 2022, being the most recent addition to the network. The story of the London Underground is not just a history of transport but a reflection of how cities grow, adapt, and innovate in response to the needs of their populations.

sections.passage:
Sleep is one of the most fundamental biological processes, yet it remains one of the least understood aspects of human physiology. We spend approximately one-third of our lives sleeping, and research has shown that sleep is far from a passive state of inactivity. Instead, it is a highly active and complex process that is essential for physical health, cognitive function, and emotional wellbeing.

Sleep occurs in cycles of approximately 90 minutes, each consisting of several distinct stages. The first stage is light sleep, during which the body begins to relax and brain waves start to slow down. This transitions into deeper sleep stages, culminating in slow-wave sleep, also known as deep sleep, which is believed to be the most restorative phase. During slow-wave sleep, the body repairs tissues, strengthens the immune system, and consolidates memories from the day. The final stage of each cycle is Rapid Eye Movement sleep, commonly known as REM sleep, during which most vivid dreaming occurs. During REM sleep, the brain is almost as active as when awake, and this stage is thought to play a crucial role in emotional processing and creative problem-solving.

The importance of sleep for cognitive function has been demonstrated in numerous studies. A landmark experiment conducted at the University of Chicago in 1999 showed that rats deprived of sleep died within two to three weeks, exhibiting symptoms of a compromised immune system. While such extreme deprivation is rare in humans, chronic sleep restriction has been linked to a wide range of health problems, including obesity, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and weakened immune function. Research by Professor Matthew Walker at the University of California, Berkeley, has shown that sleeping fewer than six hours per night is associated with a 200 percent increase in the risk of a heart attack or stroke within the next decade.

The role of sleep in learning and memory has also received considerable scientific attention. Studies have demonstrated that sleep after learning significantly improves the retention of new information. A study published in the journal Nature Neuroscience found that participants who slept after learning a new task performed 20 to 30 percent better on subsequent tests than those who stayed awake for the same period. This effect appears to be particularly strong for procedural memory — the type of memory involved in learning new skills, such as playing a musical instrument or mastering a sport.

Despite the overwhelming evidence for the importance of sleep, modern lifestyles increasingly work against healthy sleep patterns. The widespread use of electronic devices before bedtime, irregular work schedules, and the cultural glorification of busyness have all contributed to what some researchers describe as a global sleep epidemic. The World Health Organization has recommended that adults aim for seven to nine hours of sleep per night, yet surveys consistently show that a significant proportion of the population in developed countries fails to meet this recommendation.

title.zh: 文章3 - 仿生学：向自然学习

sections.passage:
Biomimicry, also known as biomimetics, is an approach to innovation that seeks sustainable solutions to human challenges by emulating nature's time-tested patterns and strategies. The core idea is that organisms, having evolved over 3.8 billion years, have already solved many of the problems that humans are grappling with today. By studying and imitating these natural designs, scientists and engineers can develop technologies that are more efficient, more sustainable, and more harmonious with the natural world.

The term biomimicry was popularized by biologist Janine Benyus in her 1997 book, Biomimicry: Innovation Inspired by Nature. However, the practice of looking to nature for design inspiration is far older. Leonardo da Vinci, for example, studied bird flight in the 15th century and produced detailed sketches of flying machines based on his observations. The Wright brothers, who achieved the first powered flight in 1903, also carefully studied the flight mechanics of birds before designing their aircraft.

One of the most famous examples of modern biomimicry is Velcro, the hook-and-loop fastener invented by Swiss engineer George de Mestral in 1941. De Mestral noticed that burrs from burdock plants clung to his dog's fur and to his clothing after a walk in the woods. Examining the burrs under a microscope, he observed that they were covered in tiny hooks that caught on the loops of fabric and fur. This observation inspired him to design a fastening system consisting of two strips of material — one with tiny hooks and the other with loops — that would stick together when pressed and pull apart easily. Velcro has since become ubiquitous in clothing, aerospace, medicine, and countless other applications.

Another compelling example is the Shinkansen bullet train in Japan. In the 1990s, engineers working on the next generation of high-speed trains faced a problem: when the trains emerged from tunnels at high speed, they created a loud sonic boom due to the sudden compression of air. The lead engineer, Eiji Nakatsu, who was also a birdwatcher, noticed that the kingfisher bird dives from the air into water with barely a splash, thanks to its long, streamlined beak. He redesigned the front of the train to resemble a kingfisher's beak, which not only solved the sonic boom problem but also reduced air resistance, making the train 15 percent faster and 10 percent more fuel-efficient.

In the field of architecture, biomimicry has inspired innovative building designs. The Eastgate Centre in Harare, Zimbabwe, designed by architect Mick Pearce, is modeled on the self-cooling mounds built by termites in sub-Saharan Africa. Termite mounds maintain a nearly constant internal temperature despite external temperatures that can vary from 3 degrees Celsius at night to over 40 degrees during the day. The building uses a similar system of ventilation channels and thermal mass to regulate temperature naturally, consuming 90 percent less energy than conventional buildings of comparable size.

Despite its enormous potential, biomimicry faces several challenges. Translating biological principles into practical engineering solutions requires interdisciplinary collaboration between biologists, engineers, and designers. Additionally, nature's designs are optimized for specific environments and constraints, and they do not always translate directly to human applications. Nevertheless, as the world faces increasingly urgent environmental challenges, biomimicry offers a promising pathway toward innovation that works with, rather than against, the natural world.

prompt.en: Some people think that the best way to reduce crime is to give longer prison sentences. Others believe there are better alternative ways of reducing crime. Discuss both views and give your own opinion. Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience. Write at least 250 words.
prompt.zh: 一些人认为减少犯罪的最好方法是延长刑期。另一些人认为有更好的替代方法来减少犯罪。讨论两种观点并给出你自己的意见。给出你回答的理由，并包括你自己的知识或经验中任何相关的例子。至少写250个单词。
